title: Millrace Overflows its Banks
deck: Three days of rain send the river over Mill Road and into the low end of Tannery Street. Residents move cars and sandbag doors.
text: The Millrace rose over its banks Monday morning, and by noon water was running across Mill Road at the footbridge and into the low end of Tannerv St. Fire crews from the Eastgate company went door to door on Tannery and Foundry streets asking families to leave by the Lower Millrace road if they could. The river crested Tuesday at 14 feet, more than four feet above the old 1972 mark, the worst flood on the Millrace since then. Water came up through basement drains and into at least thirty homes. Several garages on the south end of Tannery St. took water to the rafters of their doors. Public works crews worked through the night on the sandbag line behind the mill, which held in most places. “We have never seen it come up this fast,” said Stanley Wojcik, who has lived at the corner of Tannery and Mill for 22 years. “The water was in the kitchen before I got my boots on.” The Red Cross opened a shelter at St. Brendan’s hall, and by Wednesday afternoon some 60 people had signed in. County officials say damage assessments will begin next week. More coverage, including the south end of Tannery Street, is on pages 3 and 4.

title: Tannery Street Digs Out
deck: A month after the river went over its banks, neighbors on Tannery Street are still hauling out silt, and the cleanup has become a block project.
text: Four weeks after the Millrace went over its banks, the mud on Tannerv Street is mostly gone. What’s left is the garages. Along the south end of the street, where the river reached the rafters, the doors are off, the walls are stripped to the studs, and the tools that families couldn’t carry out are sitting in sodden piles at the curb. Ed Ostrowski’s detached garage at 318 Tannery St. was hit hardest. Ostrowski has kept a workshop in the back since 1968, and he lost a drill press, two workbenches and most of the hand tools he inherited from his father. “The drill press I can replace,” he said Saturday, standing in the doorway with a pry bar. “The drawings my father kept in the bottom drawer are gone.” Volunteers from St. Brendan’s and Scout Troop 14 came out on three Saturdays to haul debris to the county bins at the end of Mill Road. The Tannery Street block association put a sign-up sheet on every mailbox, and by the third week most houses had a shift assigned. The county has approved emergency loans for homeowners with flood damage, with an application deadline of July 15. The Red Cross relief fund at St. Brendan’s stands at $14,200. The committee will meet on June 16 at the Eastgate hall to decide how to divide it. Anyone who wants to help can bring work gloves and a wheelbarrow to the corner of Tannery and Mill on Saturday at 8 a.m. Coffee will be on the Ostrowskis’ back step.

title: Letter: Thanks to Everyone on Tannery Street
text: To the editor: I want to thank the people who showed up on the south end of Tannery Street after the flood. I came over on the first Saturday with a shovel and a borrowed pair of boots, and I was not the only one who didn’t know what I was doing. Ed and Marion Ostrowski fed everybody who came through their driveway, and the Foundry Street boys hauled more mud than anybody. The relief fund at St. Brendan’s is still open. The flood took more than furniture. It took workshops, tools, and in some cases the only car a family owned. If you can spare a check, bring it to the hall on Thursday evenings through August. Every dollar goes to the homeowners on Tannerv Street and along the lower millrace. Ruth Okafor, Tannery Flats

title: Council Approves $1.2 Million to Repair Millrace Levee
deck: Crews will rebuild the earthen levee behind Tannery Street and start on the Mill Road footbridge in March, the first major repair since the 1994 flood.
text: The Millrace Town Council voted 5–2 on Tuesday night to spend $1.2 million on repairs to the levee that runs behind Tannery Street and the Mill Road footbridge. Work is scheduled to start in March and should take about five months, weather permitting. County engineers surveyed the levee in September and found settling along a 900-foot stretch where the bank meets the millrace. Councilmember Anita Brandt, who represents Tannery Flats, said residents have asked for repairs since the spring of 2019, when heavy rain left the water within two feet of the top of the bank. The money comes from a state infrastructure grant and about $300,000 in local reserves. Two members voted against the plan, saying the council should first hold a public meeting on the footbridge’s long-term upkeep. Public comment on the work plan will be taken at the December 9 council session.

title: New Gazette Website Opens With 38 Years of Back Issues
deck: Every issue from March 1988 forward is now online, and the search tool can find names, streets and phrases in the scanned text.
text: Last month the volunteers who put this paper together launched the Millrace Gazette Online, a website that holds every issue published since March 1988. That is 452 issues, about 14,000 articles, and roughly 9,800 stories from the early years that were scanned from print and read by computer. Because those early stories were scanned from paper, the text sometimes has mistakes. “Tannery” can come out as “Tannerv,” for example, and a dot can turn into a comma. The search tool allows for small misspellings like these. Stories written on computers after 2010 come through clean. The site has no server behind it. Every page is a file, which means it loads quickly and can be copied to a new host if we ever need to move it. Volunteers will be at the Millrace Library on Saturday mornings through December to help readers search the archive and print old stories.

title: Holiday Lights Go Up on Kettle Hill
deck: Forty-two households on Orchard Lane and Kettle Hill Road have signed up for the lighting tour, which runs December 6 through January 1.
text: Walk or drive the loop from Kettle Hill Park to the top of Orchard Lane and you will see every kind of holiday display, from a single string of white bulbs on a porch rail to a sleigh and eight reindeer on a front lawn that has been wired up since 2011. Organizers ask visitors to park along the south side of Kettle Hill Road and to keep moving so the cars behind them can get through. A donation box at the park gate collects money for the Canal Park Food Pantry. Last year it took in $1,140.

title: Parking Permit Rules Revised for Foundry Row
deck: Residents who park on the street overnight will need a sticker starting in February, and guest passes will be capped at 30 a year.
text: The council approved a revised overnight parking ordinance for the Foundry Row blocks on a 6–1 vote. Stickers will cost $10 a year for the first car and $25 for a second. The city expects the new rules to start in February, after a 60-day notice period. The guest pass limit was the most debated change. Several residents said 30 passes a year is too few for households that host holiday visitors. The council agreed to revisit the cap in June.

title: Canal Park Food Pantry Moves to Larger Hall
deck: The pantry will serve Tuesday and Thursday shoppers from the St. Brendan’s Parish hall starting December 1.
text: The Canal Park Food Pantry is leaving its cramped room behind the laundromat for the parish hall on Canal Street, which has three times the floor space and a loading door that opens straight onto the lot. Shoppers will be able to pick out their own food instead of waiting in line for pre-packed bags. Volunteer coordinator Jerome Adeyemi said the new setup should cut waiting time from about 40 minutes to under 15. The pantry is still looking for two drivers for Thursday pickups.

title: Budget Hearing Draws Record Crowd of 212
deck: Most speakers asked the council to keep the library open on Sundays and to avoid cutting the bus shelter program.
text: The council’s budget hearing ran four hours, the longest in recent memory. Two hundred and twelve people signed up to speak, and the chair limited each speaker to two minutes. Many used their time to ask for the Sunday library hours to be restored. The proposed budget keeps the library at its current schedule but does not restore Sunday service. The council is expected to vote on the budget at its December 2 meeting.

title: Foxglove Heights Block Party Plans Set for Spring
deck: Residents will vote in January on a new date and a shared-cost budget for the June street fair.
text: The Foxglove Heights block party has been held on the second Saturday in June for 21 years, but the weather last spring pushed it into a rainout in two of those years. The steering group has proposed moving the party to the third Saturday of June. Each household would pay a $15 share toward tables, a bounce house and the sound system. Residents who cannot pay will not be asked to. The vote will be held at the community room on January 14.

title: Scout Troop 14 Repaints Millrace Green Benches
deck: Eleven benches around the green were sanded and repainted over two Saturdays, using paint donated by the hardware store on Mill Road.
text: Troop 14 spent the first two Saturdays of October scraping, sanding and painting the benches on Millrace Green. The boys said the hardest part was the bench nearest the bandstand, which had at least six layers of paint on it. Scoutmaster Ed Pruitt said the troop will do the same for the benches at Stonebridge Park in the spring. Anyone who wants to sponsor a bench plaque can contact the Lower Millrace Improvement Group.

title: Eastgate Elementary Wins State Reading Grant
deck: The $25,000 grant will pay for a part-time library aide and new books for grades K through 2.
text: Eastgate Elementary has been awarded a $25,000 early literacy grant from the state. Principal Denise Holloway said the money will pay for a library aide three days a week and about 800 new picture books for the primary grades. The school will hold a family reading night on January 22. Parents of kindergarten and first-grade students will receive sign-up forms in their backpacks this week.

title: Bellwood Chapel Seeks Drivers for Winter Meal Route
deck: Volunteers deliver 60 hot meals each weekday to homebound residents. The route needs four more drivers by January.
text: The Bellwood Chapel meal route has run every weekday since 1996. Drivers pick up insulated boxes at 11 a.m. and finish the route around 1 p.m. Most drivers take the same six or seven stops each week, and many have been doing it for years. Anyone with a valid license and a few hours a week can volunteer. Training takes about 40 minutes. Call the chapel office or stop by on a weekday morning.

title: Stonebridge Trail Closed for Culvert Work Through December
deck: The city will replace a stone culvert under the trail near Hickory Ridge Road. Use the Eastgate detour until the work is done.
text: The trail between Stonebridge Park and the Hickory Ridge footbridge will be closed to walkers and bikes until about December 19. The stone culvert that carries the trail over a feeder creek has cracked along its east wall, and crews need to rebuild it before the spring thaw. The detour follows Eastgate Avenue to the rail underpass and returns on the south bank. It adds about a mile. Signs are posted at both ends of the closed section.

title: Then & Now: The Mill Road Footbridge, 1971 and 2026
deck: The footbridge that will get new piers in March has carried foot traffic across the millrace for more than 50 years.
text: The steel footbridge was built in 1971 to replace a wooden span that had washed out twice in the 1960s. A county photo from that year shows the first crossing, with men in suits and children in winter coats on the new deck. Fifty-five years later the bridge is still in use, though its piers have settled and the railings have been repainted at least a dozen times. The levee work scheduled for March will rebuild the south pier and the approach ramp.

title: Council Okays Speed Bumps on Hickory Ridge Road
deck: Two raised crosswalks will go in near the elementary school after a summer of complaints from parents.
text: Two raised crosswalks will be installed on Hickory Ridge Road in front of the elementary school. The council approved $48,000 for the work on a 5–3 vote. The city will also add a painted pedestrian zone at the Orchard Lane corner. Parents said drivers routinely pass school buses on the hill. Public works says the new crosswalks should slow traffic to about 20 miles an hour in school zones.

title: Winter Concert Schedule Announced for Middle and High School
deck: Concerts run from December 10 to December 18 in the Millrace Middle School gym. Tickets are free at the door.
text: The Millrace Middle School band, chorus and string ensemble will perform on December 10, 11 and 12. The high school jazz band and show choir take the stage on December 17 and 18. All shows begin at 7 p.m. and last about 90 minutes. Doors open 30 minutes early. Seating is first come, first served, and the gym holds about 400 people.

title: Millrace Middle School Robotics Team Heads to State Finals
deck: Six students built a robot that sorts recycling. The team will compete at the state finals in February.
text: The Millrace Middle School robotics team qualified for the state finals after a second-place finish at the regional meet in October. Their robot uses a color sensor and a rotating arm to sort plastic, glass and paper from a conveyor belt. Coach Lena Park said the team meets Tuesdays and Thursdays after school. The club is always looking for mentors who can help with wiring and programming. The team is raising money through a bake sale on December 5.

title: Letter: The Levee Coverage Was Long Overdue
text: To the editor: Thank you for the front-page story on the levee. I have lived on Tannery Street since 1986 and have watched that bank slump a little more every spring. I am glad someone with a county engineering report finally put the numbers in print. I hope the council will keep the public meeting on the footbridge. Many of us who walk across it every day would like a say in what the repairs look like.

title: Letter: The Lantern Walk Brought Us Back Together
text: To the editor: Last year’s Lantern Walk was the first time in a long time that I saw my neighbors from the south end of the street at the same place at the same time. I hope this year brings even more of us out. The walk leaves Tannery Street Park at 6 p.m. on November 29 and ends at the old mill steps. Bring a flashlight if you have one. The Scouts will have lanterns for the children.

title: Ellen M. Sadowski, 84, Longtime Canal Park Librarian
deck: She ran the Canal Park branch reading room for 31 years and started the first summer story hour in the neighborhood.
text: Ellen Marie Sadowski died November 3 at Eastgate Care Center. She was 84. Born in Millrace in 1942, she joined the Canal Park branch as a part-time clerk in 1966 and became head librarian in 1979, a post she held until her retirement in 2010. She is survived by two sons, five grandchildren and a long list of former students and patrons who remember her summer story hours in the reading room. Services were held at St. Brendan’s on November 8. Donations may be made to the library’s children’s fund.

title: Frank Dwyer, 91, Eastgate Volunteer Firefighter
deck: He answered alarms for the Eastgate company for 47 years and rarely missed a Thursday drill.
text: Francis X. Dwyer, known to everyone as Frank, died October 29 at home on Eastgate Avenue. He was 91. He joined the Eastgate Volunteer Fire Co. in 1958 and served as assistant chief from 1974 to 1989. Friends remember him as the man who kept the hose house swept and the coffee on. A memorial breakfast will be held at the fire hall on December 6.

title: Holiday Events Roundup: 17 Things to Do Between Thanksgiving and New Year’s
deck: Tree lightings, lantern walks, a teen dance, skating on Marsh Landing Pond and a New Year’s countdown on Millrace Green.
text: Here is everything happening in the neighborhoods from the Saturday after Thanksgiving through the last night of the year. Times and prices come from the organizers. If the weather changes plans, check the host’s posting before you go. Events are listed in date order. Most are free. Where there is a charge, it is listed with the event.

title: Winter Market Returns to Cedar Hollow Pavilion
deck: Vendors will sell from 9 a.m. to noon on Saturdays, December 5, 12 and 19, under the pavilion roof.
text: The Cedar Hollow Winter Market returns for its third season with 14 vendors selling baked goods, wool scarves, honey, candles and holiday wreaths. Most vendors are from within 20 miles of Millrace. The market accepts cash and cards. A small table near the entrance sells the market’s wooden tokens for children to trade for a free cider.

title: Then & Now: Tannery Street’s Flood Garage, 1994 and 2026
deck: Thirty-two years after the spring flood, the garage at 318 Tannery Street has a new roof and no visible water line. Here is the spot.
text: In June 1994 the Gazette ran a series of photographs of the south end of Tannery Street after the river went over its banks. The most striking was the detached garage at 318 Tannery Street, where the water had reached the rafters of the door. The garage is still standing. Its owner, Ed Ostrowski’s grandson Nate, rebuilt the roof and the door in 2008 and added a second bay for a workbench. The water line on the back wall has been painted over, but it is still visible from the alley if you know where to look.
